Sequences dispersed around a value

Source: R/seq-disperse.R
seq_disperse.Rd

seq_disperse() creates a sequence of values around from, a given number of steps up and down, where a step is one unit of the last decimal place: 7.93 is surrounded by 7.91, 7.92, 7.94, 7.95, and so on.

seq_disperse_df() returns the sequence as a data frame column, with further columns added as in tibble::tibble(). Its arguments are those of seq_disperse() with a leading dot.

Usage

seq_disperse(
  from,
  by = NULL,
  dispersion = 1:5,
  offset_from = 0L,
  out_min = "auto",
  out_max = NULL,
  include_reported = TRUE,
  track_diff_var = FALSE
)

seq_disperse_df(
  .from,
  .by = NULL,
  ...,
  .dispersion = 1:5,
  .offset_from = 0L,
  .out_min = "auto",
  .out_max = NULL,
  .include_reported = TRUE,
  .track_diff_var = FALSE
)

Arguments

from, .from

Numeric, or a string coercible to numeric. The value to disperse from.

by, .by

Numeric. Step size. Default is NULL, in which case it is one unit of the last decimal place of from. A number does not keep trailing zeros, so 5.30 steps by 0.1: give by = 0.01, or from as the string "5.30".

dispersion, .dispersion

Numeric. Whole numbers of steps up and down from from. Default is 1:5.

offset_from, .offset_from

Integer. Moves the starting point by that many steps. Default is 0.

out_min, .out_min, out_max, .out_max

Limits on the values, including from itself. out_min defaults to "auto", one step above zero, which suits a count but not a quantity that can reach zero or be negative; use NULL for an unbounded quantity such as a mean, or 0 for one bounded at zero such as a standard deviation. out_max defaults to NULL, no maximum, and "auto" is the same.

include_reported, .include_reported

Logical. Should from itself be part of the sequence? Default is TRUE.

track_diff_var, .track_diff_var

Logical. Should the number of steps from from be returned as well? Default is FALSE. If TRUE, seq_disperse() returns a list of the sequence and the steps, and seq_disperse_df() adds a diff_var column.

...

Further columns, added as in tibble::tibble(). Only in seq_disperse_df().

Value

  • seq_disperse() returns a numeric vector, which is integer if from is an integer and every value is a whole number. With track_diff_var = TRUE, it returns a list of that vector and an integer vector of steps.

  • seq_disperse_df() returns a tibble with the sequence in the x column, the steps in diff_var if requested, and any columns added via the dots.

Details

Unlike base::seq(), these functions need not return a regular sequence: dispersion can be any non-negative whole numbers, in any order, such as c(1, 4, 9). The values follow that order, mirrored around from. Steps of 0 and repeated steps are dropped.

See also

disperse() and base::seq(), whose ideas seq_disperse() combines.

Examples

seq_disperse(from = 4.02)
#>  [1] 3.97 3.98 3.99 4.00 4.01 4.02 4.03 4.04 4.05 4.06 4.07

# A number loses trailing zeros, so state the step size:
seq_disperse(from = 5.30, by = 0.01)
#>  [1] 5.25 5.26 5.27 5.28 5.29 5.30 5.31 5.32 5.33 5.34 5.35

# More steps:
seq_disperse(from = 4.02, dispersion = 1:10)
#>  [1] 3.92 3.93 3.94 3.95 3.96 3.97 3.98 3.99 4.00 4.01 4.02 4.03 4.04 4.05 4.06
#> [16] 4.07 4.08 4.09 4.10 4.11 4.12

# Irregular steps:
seq_disperse(from = 4.02, dispersion = c(2, 3, 7))
#> [1] 3.95 3.99 4.00 4.02 4.04 4.05 4.09

# The data frame variant takes further columns:
seq_disperse_df(.from = 4.02, n = 45)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 2
#>        x     n
#>    <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  3.97    45
#>  2  3.98    45
#>  3  3.99    45
#>  4  4       45
#>  5  4.01    45
#>  6  4.02    45
#>  7  4.03    45
#>  8  4.04    45
#>  9  4.05    45
#> 10  4.06    45
#> 11  4.07    45
